solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Absolutely not what's in Rosa Klebb's shoe

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a scornful exclamation of flat disbelief
second meaning: Rosa Klebb is the setter, so what sits in her shoe is the setter's own foot

explanation.surface: A Bond fan denies that the villain Rosa Klebb hides anything in her shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosa Klebb is a Bond villain with a poisoned blade in her shoe, but here she is also the setter's pseudonym, so 'Rosa Klebb's' means 'mine'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal British retort used to dismiss a claim as complete nonsense.

clue.text: Beginning to despair, constricted by comparatively tight snake

indicators.note: constricted means squeezed in, so one piece is held tight inside another
the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

explanation.surface: A victim begins to lose hope as a snake coils ever tighter around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snake' reads as the creature, fitting 'constricted', but it is a verb meaning to wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A river or path that winds along a twisting course is said to snake.

clue.text: Jolly lady with extremely neat buttocks

parts.note: a jolly is a fun outing

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

explanation.surface: A cheerful woman has a very trim rear.
explanation.definitionFit: This rather formal or jocular word refers to the bottom, the part of the body one sits on.

clue.text: Awards ceremony on Saturday initially held up by traffic

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is held up sits on top, so this piece comes above the next
the initials are first letters, so only the opening letter of each preceding word is kept

parts.note: the first letters of both words
road traffic is made of cars

explanation.surface: A prize-giving at the weekend is delayed by road congestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up by traffic' reads as delayed, but in a down answer it means sitting on top of the cars.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Awards in Hollywood are popularly known by the nickname of their statuette.

clue.text: Hunts and kills poor dear pets

indicators.note: something in poor shape has been knocked about, so the following words come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A cat owner laments that their animals stalk and slaughter beloved household pets.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal that preys on others is said to do this, the verb behind the noun predator.

clue.text: Orgy over in conservatoire

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the letters are read backwards
the letters sit inside the next word rather than being built from parts

parts.note: found inside the last part of the word

explanation.surface: A wild party is happening inside a music college.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy of colour or violence is an unrestrained outburst, just as a wild profusion is.

clue.text: Reject and insult everyone that hurt me

explanation.surface: Someone snubbed and abused by everyone complains of the pain.
explanation.definitionFit: A referee who refuses to accept a goal is turning it down as invalid.

clue.text: Taking offence daily

wordplay.note: the daily paper that prints this puzzle, the Financial Times, with its definite article

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking offence' looks like being upset, but it is the crime of taking; the daily is THE FT, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealing is the criminal act of taking property, so it is literally an offence of taking.

clue.text: One's underneath bulk of male escort, wriggling

indicators.note: the bulk is most but not all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down clue, a piece underneath another is written after it

parts.note: one's and my are both possessives of the speaker

explanation.surface: A gigolo's client lies beneath him, writhing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fidgets and twists about uncomfortably is restless and wriggly.

clue.text: Some peculiar Nicaraguan herbal remedy

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are wanted, a run taken from inside the words

parts.note: spans the end of peculiar and the start of Nicaraguan

explanation.surface: An odd Central American plant cure is being described.
explanation.definitionFit: This mountain flower is made into creams and tinctures used by herbalists for bruises and sprains.

clue.text: Open University dons assure worried philosopher

indicators.note: a word that is worried is worked at and pulled about, so its letters get rearranged
to don is to put on, so one set of letters is slipped onto and into another

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for Britain's distance-learning university

explanation.surface: Lecturers at a correspondence university reassure an anxious thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university lecturers, fitting the Open University, but it is the verb meaning puts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was the Genevan Enlightenment thinker who wrote The Social Contract.

clue.text: Push out old Benedict, disheartened and humble

indicators.note: with the heart removed, only the outer letters of the name remain

parts.note: as in a rude hut, simple and lowly

explanation.surface: An old monk called Benedict is discouraged and meek.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrust something forward so that it sticks out is to make it protrude.

clue.text: Reported terrible social division and vituperation

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound of the next words matters

parts.note: dire is terrible and a tribe is a social division

explanation.surface: A news story covers a dreadful split in society and the abuse that goes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter, sustained verbal attack is a form of harsh abusive criticism.

clue.text: Intermittently unnoticed, unless they're in Paisley area

indicators.note: if every other letter goes unnoticed, only the alternating remainder is read

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth and eleventh letters

explanation.surface: Something passes unseen unless people are in the Scottish town of Paisley.
explanation.walkthrough: Paisley looks like the town near Glasgow, but it is Ian Paisley, the Northern Irish Protestant leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Paisley's political base was the province of Northern Ireland, often called by this historic provincial name.

clue.text: Hand vino to a drunk

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of line, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone passes wine to a drunkard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' reads as a verb, pass, but it is the noun, as in give them a big hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A round of applause, as in 'give them a big hand', is a burst of clapping.

clue.text: Broadcast bounder's regrets

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard over the air, so the following word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a bounder is a cad, and a roué is a dissolute rake

explanation.surface: A cad's apologies are aired on radio.
explanation.walkthrough: A bounder is old British slang for a dishonourable man, much like a roué.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel sorrow or repentance about something is to lament it, an old-fashioned verb still common in phrases.

clue.text: Dislocated your pelvis once

indicators.note: a dislocated joint is out of place, so these letters are moved out of their order

explanation.surface: A doctor tells a patient they had a hip injury at some point in the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean at an earlier time, before now.

clue.text: Moody aunties angrily inhaling Senior Service

indicators.note: in a temper things get thrown about, so the letters come out disordered
to inhale is to draw in, so one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: the Royal Navy, the oldest of the British armed services

explanation.surface: Grumpy aunts furiously smoke Senior Service cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: Senior Service was a British cigarette brand, which fits 'inhaling', but it is also the nickname of the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: A gloomy, sullen temperament was once blamed on the influence of the planet Saturn.

clue.text: Stress of priest taken in by false messiah

indicators.note: something false is not genuine, so the word is reworked into a different arrangement
to be taken in is to be drawn inside, so one piece sits within another

explanation.surface: A clergyman suffers the strain of being fooled by a fake saviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Special importance or weight placed on something, such as a syllable, is accent or stress.

clue.text: Chum clipping flanks of ill- tempered cow

indicators.note: a clip holds something in its grip, so one piece is gripped inside another
the flanks are the sides, so only the two outer letters of the following word count

explanation.surface: A friend restrains the sides of an angry cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' reads as a farm animal but is the verb meaning to browbeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to frighten them into submission, which is the same as browbeating them.

clue.text: Motivation of international politician in France and America

explanation.surface: What drives a global statesman working in France and the USA?
explanation.definitionFit: The driving force or momentum behind an action is its stimulus or incentive.

clue.text: Withdrawing objections is a bit of a fag

indicators.note: withdrawing means drawing back, so the word is read in the backward direction

explanation.surface: Taking back your complaints is a bit of a chore.
explanation.walkthrough: A fag is British slang for a cigarette, and also for a tiresome task, which is the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The end left over from a smoked cigarette is the small remaining part of it.

clue.text: Bloody lucky!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a mild euphemistic intensifier, as in every last day
second meaning: fortunate, favoured by heaven

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one exclamation, 'very fortunate!', but the two words are separate meanings; bloody is a British swear-word intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as a polite substitute for a curse and also describes someone who is fortunate or favoured.

clue.text: Hostile states finally negotiate

indicators.note: at the very end, so only the closing letter of the next word counts

explanation.surface: Enemy nations at last sit down to talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like nations, but it is the verb meaning declares.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone strongly opposed to or disinclined towards something is unfriendly to it.

clue.text: Lavish bonus starts to hearten you

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are taken

explanation.surface: A generous bonus at the start would cheer you up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something luxurious and opulent, like a velvety plush furnishing, is lavish.

clue.text: Part of Italy without single area of shade

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is removed

explanation.surface: A region of Italy lacks any one shady spot.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy and optics this Latin term names the darkest central part of a shadow.

clue.text: Meet leader of conspiracy by side of road

indicators.note: the leader stands at the front, so the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: by and on both mean beside or next to
the grass strip along the edge of a road

explanation.surface: A plotter's ringleader arranges a rendezvous at the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the verge is the strip of grass beside a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines or people that come together from different directions are said to meet at one point.

clue.text: Bother doctor over a temperature

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece over another is written above it, so first

explanation.surface: A patient pesters the GP about a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bother' looks like a verb, pester, but it is the mild exclamation of annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild old-fashioned exclamations of irritation used instead of stronger swearing.

clue.text: Tense and guarded, regularly following orders no doubt

indicators.note: coming after, so the piece before this word is placed after the next one

parts.note: Officers of the Order of the British Empire, a British honour

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter of the preceding word is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Nervous and cautious, someone is unquestionably obeying instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orders' suggests commands, but it means honours: the OBE is a British order of chivalry.
explanation.definitionFit: This stock Irish-sounding phrase is an emphatic way of saying certainly or of course.

clue.text: Intellectuals at home wearing women's underwear

indicators.note: whatever is worn wraps around the wearer, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: being in means being at home

explanation.surface: Clever people lounge about the house in lingerie.
explanation.definitionFit: The cleverest people in a group are informally called its thinkers or masterminds.

clue.text: Dearth of sex, years after fights

indicators.note: placed later in sequence, so the pieces named before it come behind the one named after it

parts.note: a coy word for sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: After years of quarrelling, a couple's love life has dried up.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcity or thinness of supply is a shortage, the sense of a dearth.

clue.text: Saw Rachel half-cut in the sack

indicators.note: with half cut away, only one half of the name survives
something in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to hit the sack is to go to bed
the second half of the name

explanation.surface: Someone spotted Rachel drunk in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for drunk, which is the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are past tense forms of verbs meaning to look at or observe something.
